The historical problem

Cosmopolitan exchange did not erase social hierarchy.

Planned

Wards, markets, gates, and palaces organized urban life.

Connected

Envoys, merchants, monks, artisans, and entertainers crossed regions.

Unequal

Exams widened recruitment, but education, office, and family networks remained uneven.

Argument: Chang’an was a hub of Asian exchange because Tang power organized movement. The same state also ranked families and controlled access to office.

This slide asks you to focus on the lecture’s central claim: openness and inequality existed at the same time. Read the evidence as part of a larger historical relationship, not as an isolated fact. As you work through the slide, notice who could move, worship, trade, study, or gain office—and what limits still shaped those choices.

A planned city did not simply welcome everyone equally. Officials supervised markets and gates, the court licensed religious institutions, and elite families invested in education and marriage ties. Examinations mattered increasingly, but they did not make Tang society a modern meritocracy. Pay attention to dates, labels, and cautions because they show what historians know securely and where estimates or later traditions need qualification. Holding both sides together produces a stronger argument than calling Tang China either completely open or completely closed. Sui plan · Tang capital

Chang’an placed imperial authority at the north.

  • The Sui founded Daxing in 583; the Tang renamed it Chang’an.
  • A rectangular grid divided the city into 108 residential wards.
  • The palace and imperial city occupied the north-central axis.
  • Two supervised markets served different parts of the city.

Daily rhythm

Walls and gates regulated movement.

Wards

Residents entered neighborhoods through gates; rules and curfews changed over time and were not always obeyed.

Markets

Officials supervised trade, weights, prices, and merchant activity in the east and west markets.

A gridded city created order on paper. Everyday practice was messier: residents, officials, visitors, and businesses adapted the rules.

This slide asks you to focus on how built space and administrative rules shaped ordinary movement. Read the evidence as part of a larger historical relationship, not as an isolated fact. Wards should not be imagined as identical modern blocks. They contained homes, temples, offices, gardens, and lodging. Curfews and gate rules mattered, but enforcement varied across time. Market supervision linked commerce to state authority. A dual-capital system

Chang’an and Luoyang served different strategic needs.

Chang’anLuoyang
Primary dynastic capital; close to the northwestern military and aristocratic baseEastern capital; closer to the Grand Canal, grain routes, and the populous North China Plain
Symbolic center of Tang rule and foreign embassiesUsed heavily when supply or court politics drew rulers east

Population caution: Chang’an was among the world’s largest cities, but precise totals—especially “two million”—depend on uncertain boundaries and estimates.

Chang’an’s western location connected it to the dynasty’s military base and continental routes, while Luoyang sat closer to canal-borne grain and eastern population centers. Emperors moved between them rather than treating Luoyang as merely a lesser copy. Religious communities

Presence did not mean mass conversion.

Before TangZoroastrian communities already served Iranian diasporas

694Manichaean teachers appear at court
8th c.Muslim merchants are better documented in southern ports than at Chang’an

Buddhism and Daoism had far broader institutions and followings. Evidence for a Tang Jewish community in Chang’an is too thin for a confident claim.

This slide asks you to focus on careful distinctions among foreign religious communities, court recognition, and wider conversion. Zoroastrianism, the Church of the East, and Manichaeism were closely tied to migrant communities and sometimes received court permission. Islam reached China through maritime and diplomatic contacts, but evidence is stronger for port cities such as Guangzhou than for early Tang Chang’an. Judaism should not be placed confidently in the capital without firmer evidence. Material culture

Tang elites adopted and remade foreign styles.

  • Polo, associated with Iranian and Central Asian courts, became fashionable among Tang men and women.
  • Music and dance drew on performers and instruments from Central, South, and West Asia.
  • Metalwork shapes and motifs inspired Chinese ceramics and luxury goods.
  • Adoption changed meanings; borrowing was not simple copying.

Tang tomb mural of polo players, c. 706 · public domain.

This slide asks you to focus on how objects and performances reveal selective cultural borrowing. Read the evidence as part of a larger historical relationship, not as an isolated fact. As you work through the slide, notice who could move, worship, trade, study, or gain office—and what limits still shaped those choices.

The mural makes exchange visible without assuming that every Tang resident played polo or wore foreign clothing. Court and aristocratic consumers had the wealth and access to turn imported practices into prestige. Artisans also adapted foreign forms into locally made goods. Pay attention to dates, labels, and cautions because they show what historians know securely and where estimates or later traditions need qualification. A source with a purpose

The Xi’an Stele tells a Christian community’s story.

“The illustrious religion spread through the Middle Kingdom.”
  • Written in Chinese with Syriac names.
  • Recalls Aluoben’s arrival in 635 and imperial approval.
  • Uses Chinese religious vocabulary to explain Christian ideas.
  • Celebrates the community; it is not a neutral census.

The inscription is invaluable because it records people, dates, imperial actions, and a Christian effort to communicate in Chinese terms. Yet its authors wanted to honor their religion and patrons. The phrase on the slide is a short paraphrase rather than a claim that Christianity dominated China. From Nine Ranks to Tang recruitment

The Sui ended a formal ranking system, not family advantage.

220sNine-Rank system classifies candidates through local evaluators
4th–6th c.Great families increasingly dominate rankings and office
SuiCentralized appointments and examinations replace Nine-Rank procedures
TangMultiple recruitment paths coexist
Abolishing a rule is not the same as erasing the education, wealth, reputation, and networks families had built.

Elite culture

Families converted resources into reputation.

  • Education prepared sons for exams, writing, and courtly communication.
  • Marriage connected lineages and strengthened political networks.
  • Genealogies advertised ancestry and protected claims to status.
  • Residence in the capitals increased access to patrons and information.
Elite identity shifted toward learning and office, but access to those achievements still depended heavily on family resources.

This slide asks you to focus on the mechanisms that allowed elite families to reproduce advantage even when formal rules changed. Read the evidence as part of a larger historical relationship, not as an isolated fact. As you work through the slide, notice who could move, worship, trade, study, or gain office—and what limits still shaped those choices.

Money alone did not guarantee office, but it paid for tutors, books, travel, and time to study. Marriage ties connected households, genealogies made claims legible, and capital residence brought candidates closer to patrons and examinations. These were social investments. Synthesis

Chang’an concentrated connections—and controlled access.

Across Asia

Routes brought migrants, diplomats, religions, objects, and performances into Tang cities.

Within the empire

Palaces, markets, schools, exams, family privilege, and court rankings organized who gained influence.

Takeaway: cosmopolitanism describes circulation and contact. It does not, by itself, describe equality.

This slide asks you to focus on the final connection between the city’s international networks and its internal social hierarchy. Read the evidence as part of a larger historical relationship, not as an isolated fact. As you work through the slide, notice who could move, worship, trade, study, or gain office—and what limits still shaped those choices.

Urban planning and court policy helped create the conditions for exchange, while the same institutions supervised markets, licensed communities, ranked lineages, and selected officials. Movement could expand choices without distributing power evenly. Pay attention to dates, labels, and cautions because they show what historians know securely and where estimates or later traditions need qualification. If a dotted term appears, you can open it for added context without losing the slide’s main argument.

Key terms

Keep these distinctions in view.

Urban space

Ward · gated city district
Dual capitals · Chang’an and Luoyang

Exchange

Cosmopolitan · shaped by contacts across regions
Diaspora · community living away from an ancestral homeland

Elite

Nine Ranks · earlier candidate classification
Yin privilege · eligibility inherited from an official father

This slide asks you to focus on six terms that organize the lecture rather than serving as a memorization list. Read the evidence as part of a larger historical relationship, not as an isolated fact. As you work through the slide, notice who could move, worship, trade, study, or gain office—and what limits still shaped those choices.

Ward and dual capitals describe space; cosmopolitan and diaspora describe patterns of connection; Nine Ranks and yin privilege describe institutions of status. Pairing each term with a category helps you retrieve it in an argument. Pay attention to dates, labels, and cautions because they show what historians know securely and where estimates or later traditions need qualification. Five-minute writing activity · work on your own

Explain the tension at the heart of Tang Chang’an.

How did foreign interactions and long-distance routes shape Chang’an’s cultural and religious landscape, and why did that openness not eliminate elite hierarchy?

Write 5–7 sentences. Use one feature of the city, two examples of cultural or religious contact, and one mechanism of elite advantage. End with a judgment: was the court mainly an organizer, a gatekeeper, or both?

Adapted from Review Question 3 in the course textbook, ch. 5.

This slide asks you to focus on a short evidence-based explanation that joins the lecture’s urban, cultural, and social themes. Read the evidence as part of a larger historical relationship, not as an isolated fact. As you work through the slide, notice who could move, worship, trade, study, or gain office—and what limits still shaped those choices.

Begin with a claim, then make each example do analytical work. A city feature might be the markets or ward system. Contact examples could include Sogdian communities, the Church of the East, polo, music, or adapted luxury goods. Elite mechanisms include education, yin privilege, marriage, genealogies, and capital residence. Pay attention to dates, labels, and cautions because they show what historians know securely and where estimates or later traditions need qualification. If a dotted term appears, you can open it for added context without losing the slide’s main argument.

Your final judgment should explain how the court could enable exchange and regulate it at the same time.
